subject: Business Models
title: Genomics-Based Services
description: A quick, practical guide to Genomics-Based Services.

hook.text: Sequencing a human genome cost $3 billion in 2003. Today it costs $200. The price collapse created an industry.

buildup.text: 23andMe, Nebula Genomics, and Color offer genetic testing for ancestry, health risks, and drug responses.

discovery.text: Pharmacogenomics matches medications to your genetics. The right drug for your DNA, not trial and error.

twist.text: 23andMe nearly went bankrupt in 2024. Selling genetic data is controversial and one-time testing limits repeat revenue.

climax.text: Genomics will transform medicine, but the consumer business model—testing once, selling data—is still proving itself.

punchline.text: $3B in 2003, $200 today. Cheap genomes, uncertain business model.

quiz.question: What business model challenge does 23andMe face?
options: One-time genetic testing has limited repeat revenue potential

details.summary: Genomics-based services use DNA sequencing data to provide personalized health insights, ancestry information, pharmacogenomic guidance, and disease risk assessment..
details.whyItMatters: As genome sequencing costs have dropped from 3 billion dollars to under 200 dollars, genomics services are becoming mass market..
takeaways: DNA sequencing provides personalized health, ancestry, and drug response data
Sequencing costs have dropped over 99.99% enabling mass market services
Pharmacogenomics matches drug treatments to individual genetic profiles

faq.question: How do genomics companies monetize genetic data?
faq.answer: Consumer testing fees ranging from $99 to $299 for health and ancestry reports. Subscription services for ongoing health insights. Pharmaceutical company partnerships for drug development research. Enterprise health screening programs for employers and insurers..

faq.question: What privacy concerns surround genomics-based services?
faq.answer: Genetic data is permanently identifying and cannot be changed if exposed. Law enforcement has used consumer DNA databases to solve crimes. Insurance companies could discriminate based on genetic risk. Data breaches could expose immutable personal health information..
